title: Unit 2: Cells

topics.name: Tonicity, water potential, and osmoregulation
covers: Cell regulatory mechanisms (like osmosis and selective permeability)

guide.title: Cells: review guide
guide.intro: Cells are the basic units of life. This unit links organelles to their jobs, explains why cells are small, shows how the plasma membrane controls what enters and leaves, and describes how internal membranes divide the work of eukaryotic cells.
guide.equationNote: Solute potential: Ψs = −iCRT, with R = 0.0831 L·bar/(mol·K) and T in kelvins. Water potential: Ψ = Ψs + Ψp.

sections.title: Cell structure, function, and size
body: Organelles have specific jobs: ribosomes make proteins; the rough ER (studded with ribosomes) makes proteins for membranes and secretion; the Golgi modifies and packages them; mitochondria carry out most of cellular respiration; chloroplasts carry out photosynthesis; lysosomes digest materials; vacuoles store water and other substances.

As a cell grows, its volume increases faster than its surface area, so its surface area-to-volume ratio falls. Exchange with the environment happens across the surface, so small cells, and shapes that are flat, thin, or folded (such as microvilli), exchange materials more efficiently.
points: A cube with side s has SA = 6s² and V = s³, so SA/V = 6/s.
Cells that secrete lots of protein have lots of rough ER and Golgi.
Ribosomes are found in all cells, including prokaryotes.

sections.title: The plasma membrane and transport
body: The plasma membrane is a phospholipid bilayer with embedded proteins (the fluid mosaic model). It is selectively permeable: small nonpolar molecules (O₂, CO₂) diffuse straight through, while ions and larger polar molecules need transport proteins.

Passive transport (simple diffusion, and facilitated diffusion through channels or carriers such as aquaporins) moves substances down their concentration gradient without using energy. Active transport, such as the Na⁺/K⁺ pump, uses energy (often ATP) to move substances against their gradient. Large materials enter by endocytosis and leave by exocytosis, in vesicles.
points: Facilitated diffusion is still passive: no ATP.
Pumps create gradients; channels let substances run down them.
Cells secrete proteins such as insulin by exocytosis.

sections.title: Tonicity, water potential, and osmoregulation
body: Water moves by osmosis toward the side with more solute. In a hypotonic solution a cell gains water (animal cells may burst; plant cells become firm against their walls). In a hypertonic solution it loses water (plant cells plasmolyze). In an isotonic solution there is no net movement.
Water potential (Ψ) predicts direction: water moves from higher to lower Ψ. Ψ = Ψs + Ψp; adding solute makes Ψs more negative (Ψs = −iCRT, where i is the number of particles each solute unit forms).
points: Pure water at atmospheric pressure has Ψ = 0.
Sucrose doesn't ionize (i = 1); NaCl gives i ≈ 2.
Freshwater protists use contractile vacuoles to pump out extra water.

sections.title: Compartmentalization and its origins
body: Eukaryotic cells have membrane-bound organelles that separate incompatible reactions (for example, lysosomes keep digestive enzymes away from the rest of the cell) and provide large internal membrane surfaces, such as the folded inner membrane of a mitochondrion. Prokaryotes lack membrane-bound organelles but have ribosomes and a plasma membrane.

Endosymbiotic theory: mitochondria and chloroplasts descended from prokaryotes engulfed by an ancestral cell. Evidence: they have double membranes, their own circular DNA, and bacteria-like ribosomes, and they divide like bacteria.
points: Folded membranes (cristae, thylakoids) increase surface area for reactions.
Prokaryotic DNA sits in a nucleoid region, not a nucleus.
Compartments let a cell keep different conditions, such as pH, in different places.

example.prompt: A cube-shaped cell grows from 1 µm to 2 µm on each side. How does its surface area-to-volume ratio change?
example.solution: At 1 µm: SA = 6 µm², V = 1 µm³, so SA/V = 6. At 2 µm: SA = 24 µm², V = 8 µm³, so SA/V = 3. The ratio halves, so each unit of volume has half as much membrane for exchange.

misconceptions: Their surface area-to-volume ratio is lower, so exchange is less efficient.
It is passive; only active transport uses energy.
Water moves toward higher solute concentration (lower water potential).
All cells have ribosomes; prokaryotes lack membrane-bound organelles.

questions.prompt: In which organelle does most of cellular respiration's ATP production happen?
questions.explanation: The citric acid cycle and the electron transport chain, which make most of the ATP, are in mitochondria.
choiceExplanations: The Golgi modifies and packages proteins.
Chloroplasts carry out photosynthesis.
The nucleus holds DNA.

questions.prompt: Cells that secrete large amounts of antibody protein have an especially large amount of which organelle?
questions.explanation: The rough ER's ribosomes make proteins destined for secretion.
choiceExplanations: Lysosomes digest materials.
Central vacuoles are found in plant cells and store water.
Smooth ER makes lipids and detoxifies; it has no ribosomes.

questions.prompt: A cube-shaped cell grows from 1 µm to 2 µm on each side. What happens to its surface area-to-volume ratio?
choices: It rises from 6 to 12 per µm
It falls from 6 to 1.5 per µm
It falls from 6 to 3 per µm
questions.explanation: SA/V = 6s²/s³ = 6/s, so it goes from 6/1 = 6 to 6/2 = 3.
choiceExplanations: Volume grows faster than surface area, so the ratio falls.
The ratio depends on size.
1.5 would be the ratio for a 4 µm cube.

questions.prompt: Cell X is a 4 µm cube. Cell Y is a 1 µm × 4 µm × 16 µm box. Both have a volume of 64 µm³. Which exchanges materials with its surroundings more efficiently, and why?
choices: Both equally, because they have the same volume
Cell X, because its surface area-to-volume ratio is larger
Cell X, because a cube has the largest surface area for its volume
Cell Y, because its surface area-to-volume ratio is larger (about 2.6 vs 1.5 per µm)
questions.explanation: X: SA = 96 µm², SA/V = 1.5. Y: SA = 2(4 + 16 + 64) = 168 µm², SA/V ≈ 2.6. Flattened shapes have more surface per unit of volume.
choiceExplanations: With equal volumes, the shape still changes the surface area.
Cell X's ratio (1.5) is smaller than cell Y's (about 2.6).
Among boxes, a cube has the smallest surface area for its volume, not the largest.

questions.prompt: Which molecule crosses a phospholipid bilayer most easily by simple diffusion?
questions.explanation: Small nonpolar molecules such as O₂ pass between the hydrophobic tails.
choiceExplanations: Charged ions can't cross the hydrophobic interior without a transport protein.
Proteins are far too large; they cross by endocytosis or exocytosis.
Glucose is large and polar, so it needs a carrier.

questions.prompt: Glucose enters a red blood cell through a carrier protein, moving from higher to lower concentration. What kind of transport is this?
questions.explanation: It uses a transport protein but moves down the gradient, so no energy is needed.
choiceExplanations: Exocytosis moves materials out of the cell in vesicles.
Active transport moves substances against their gradient using energy.
Simple diffusion doesn't use a protein.

questions.prompt: The Na⁺/K⁺ pump moves Na⁺ out of a cell and K⁺ in, both against their concentration gradients. What does it require?
choices: A higher concentration of Na⁺ inside the cell
No energy, because ions move by diffusion
questions.explanation: Moving ions against their gradients is active transport, powered by ATP hydrolysis.
choiceExplanations: The pump moves single ions through a protein, not in vesicles.
It moves Na⁺ out against its gradient; it doesn't need Na⁺ to be higher inside.
Diffusion only moves substances down their gradients.

questions.prompt: Some cells have many aquaporins in their membranes. What effect does this have?
choices: They pump water against its gradient using ATP
Water crosses their membranes much faster
Ions move faster through their membranes
questions.explanation: Aquaporins are water channels that allow rapid facilitated diffusion of water.
choiceExplanations: They increase water permeability.
Aquaporins are passive channels; water still moves by osmosis.
Aquaporins are specific to water.

questions.prompt: A poison stops a cell from making ATP. Which process stops most directly?
choices: Diffusion of O₂ into the cell
Facilitated diffusion of glucose down its gradient
Pumping Na⁺ out of the cell against its gradient
questions.explanation: Active transport depends on ATP. The other processes are passive and continue while gradients last.
choiceExplanations: O₂ diffuses through the bilayer without energy.
Osmosis through aquaporins needs no ATP.
Facilitated diffusion needs no ATP.

questions.prompt: An animal cell is placed in a hypotonic solution. What happens?
choices: Solutes rush out of the cell
Water enters the cell, and it may swell and burst
Nothing, because there is no net water movement
Water leaves the cell and it shrinks
questions.explanation: A hypotonic solution has a lower solute concentration than the cell, so water moves in by osmosis.
choiceExplanations: Osmosis is the movement of water; solutes can't cross freely.
That describes an isotonic solution.
That happens in a hypertonic solution.

questions.prompt: A plant cell is placed in a very salty (hypertonic) solution. What is the most likely result?
choices: Plasmolysis: the cell loses water and its membrane pulls away from the wall
Salt is pumped into the central vacuole until it bursts
questions.explanation: Water leaves the cell toward the higher solute concentration outside, so the cytoplasm shrinks away from the rigid wall.
choiceExplanations: The wall prevents bursting, and here water is leaving.
The cell loses water; it doesn't take on enough salt to burst.
Turgor increases in a hypotonic solution, not a hypertonic one.

questions.prompt: Solution A has a water potential of −0.2 MPa and solution B −0.6 MPa. They are separated by a membrane permeable only to water. Which way does water move?
choices: It can't be predicted from water potential
Equally in both directions, with no net movement
questions.explanation: Water moves from higher (less negative) to lower (more negative) water potential: from −0.2 to −0.6 MPa.
choiceExplanations: Water potential is exactly what predicts the direction.
This goes from lower to higher water potential.
The water potentials differ, so there is net movement.

questions.prompt: What is the solute potential of a 0.10 M sucrose solution at 295 K? (Ψs = −iCRT, R = 0.0831 L·bar/(mol·K))
questions.explanation: Sucrose doesn't ionize, so i = 1: Ψs = −(1)(0.10)(0.0831)(295) = −2.45 bar.
choiceExplanations: Solute potential is never positive; solutes lower water potential.
−0.245 bar uses 0.010 M instead of 0.10 M.
−4.90 bar uses i = 2, but sucrose doesn't split into ions.

questions.explanation: All cells have ribosomes; prokaryotes lack membrane-bound organelles.
choiceExplanations: Mitochondria are membrane-bound organelles found in eukaryotes.
The ER is a eukaryotic membrane system.
Prokaryotic DNA is in a nucleoid region, not a membrane-bound nucleus.

questions.prompt: Why is it an advantage for a cell to keep its digestive (hydrolytic) enzymes inside lysosomes?
choices: It keeps the enzymes away from the cell's other molecules and lets them work at the lysosome's acidic pH
It makes the enzymes work faster in the cytosol
It lets the enzymes leave the cell more easily
questions.explanation: Compartmentalization separates reactions that would damage the cell and keeps conditions suited to each process.
choiceExplanations: The enzymes stay inside the lysosome, not in the cytosol.
Lysosomes digest materials; they don't make ATP.
Lysosomal enzymes are meant to stay inside the cell's lysosomes.

questions.prompt: Which observation supports the idea that mitochondria descended from bacteria engulfed by an ancestral cell?
choices: Mitochondria are found in nearly all eukaryotic cells
Mitochondria are surrounded by the cell's cytoplasm
Mitochondria have their own circular DNA and bacteria-like ribosomes
questions.explanation: Circular DNA, bacterial-type ribosomes, double membranes, and division by fission all resemble free-living bacteria.
choiceExplanations: Being widespread doesn't show where they came from.
Every organelle is surrounded by cytoplasm.
Making ATP describes their function, not their origin.

questions.prompt: The inner membrane of a mitochondrion is folded into many cristae. How does this benefit the cell?
choices: It lets the mitochondrion divide faster
It increases the membrane surface area for the electron transport chain and ATP synthase, so more ATP can be made
It keeps oxygen out of the mitochondrion
questions.explanation: The proteins of the electron transport chain and ATP synthase sit in the inner membrane, so more membrane area means more of them.
choiceExplanations: Folding doesn't control the rate of division.
Mitochondrial DNA is in the matrix, not stored in the folds.
Oxygen is needed inside, as the final electron acceptor.
